look_here_first: Start with several mature blue-green, glaucous leaves—not a single shade leaf. A broadly rounded or notched tip, pale papery/scaly bark, and a barrel-shaped nut whose ends can look flattened are the useful combination. If the plant is shrubby, compare the twig and cupule carefully with white shin oak.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Small deciduous tree, often on limestone hills, canyons, streamsides, and Edwards Plateau woodlands.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Blue-green/glaucous, obovate or elliptic; margin entire to shallowly lobed; underside whitish/glaucous with stellate hairs when young.

key_traits.label: Acorn
key_traits.text: Cup shallow; nut oblong or barrel-shaped and often flattened at both ends.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: FNA: leaf blade typically 40–90 × 30–60 mm; elliptic to obovate, very blue-green and glaucous, usually rounded or retuse at the tip; shade leaves can be deeply lobed.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Leaf underside initially with erect stellate hairs that often shed as the leaf matures, leaving a pale glaucous surface; do not require permanent dense hairs.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Twigs initially erect-stellate pubescent, later glabrous; mature buds 1.5–3 mm long.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Mature acorn typically oblong/barrel-like, 13–15 mm long (range 11–20 mm), often flattened at both ends; cup 4–7 mm deep, moderately tuberculate and enclosing at most about 1/3 nut.

key_traits.label: Joey field note
key_traits.text: Joey's West Texas landscaping frame is an excellent field example of the blue-green/glaucous leaf surface and lobed foliage. Use that glaucous cast as an early cue, then confirm bark and acorn characters.
